criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community water supply and sanitation (WSS) / basic sanitation service access across urban and rural areas and municipalities in Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Satisfied, as the paper discusses legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance arrangements in Brazil's basic sanitation sector, including PLANASA, the 1988 Federal Constitution, the Public Consortia Law (Law No. 11,107 of 2005), and the National Sanitation Law (Law No. 11,445 of 2007). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Partially touches on rule-type institutional mechanisms—specifically utility ownership and regulatory/concession structure (municipalities granting concessions to provincial state-owned WSS utilities versus municipal autarchies) and cost-recovery/cross-subsidy rules under PLANASA—alongside broader macro-governance 'systemic conditions'. However, these mechanisms are discussed only in a macro-historical narrative overview rather than an empirical analysis, so the study fails Criterion 3 regardless of whether Criterion 2 is read broadly or narrowly.
criterion_notes.c3: No empirical evidence or systematic empirical synthesis. The paper is a narrative historical, institutional, and public-policy overview/essay that cites descriptive secondary statistics (e.g., IBGE 2000a, 2000b; Costa 2003; Rezende 2005) and summarizes recent legislation without any empirical research design, primary data collection, or analytical methodology; the author explicitly notes that it is a preliminary assessment ahead of ongoing empirical research. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Cites descriptive national indicators relevant to urban and rural water supply coverage, sewerage coverage, unserved population counts, and water treatment/potability risks from secondary IBGE sources.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails because there is no identifiable empirical study design, no analytical sample, and no operationalized empirical test linking an exposure to an access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: Based on the IBGE data, WSS coverage in urban areas rose about 4.5 percentage points (from 87 to 91.4 per cent) in the period 1991–2003 urban population, while, even more significantly, in rural areas it rose from 9.3 to 25 per cent, an increase of over 16 percentage points.

This was institutionalised through the establishment of a contractual relationship between the municipalities and the state governments, whereby municipalities grant the concession to provide WSS in their jurisdictions to state-owned utilities
However, arguably the most important legislative innovation in the BS sector was introduced in 2007 with the passing of the first National Sanitation Law (Law No. 11,445)

As a note of caution, due to the limits imposed by the length of the article, this analysis presents only a preliminary assessment that is being developed in greater depth both theoretically and methodologically in our ongoing research work, involving case studies and comparative analysis of public policies and management models of BS provision in Brazil.

This paper has attempted a critical examination of traditional and new technological indicators for the assessment of BS, introducing elements from public policy in what is conventionally a technical debate.

raw_response.exposure: Institutional, political, and legal arrangements in Brazil's basic sanitation sector (PLANASA state-utility concession model, tariff self-sustainability/cross-subsidy rules, and National Sanitation Law No. 11,445 of 2007), discussed narratively without empirical exposure measurement
raw_response.outcome: Urban and rural water supply and sewerage coverage rates and unserved population counts cited descriptively from secondary IBGE statistics
raw_response.population_and_sample: Population and districts/municipalities of Brazil cited via secondary national statistics (IBGE 2000 Census and 2000 National Survey of Basic Sanitation); no primary or analytical study sample
raw_response.rationale: Full-text review of Heller (2007) confirms that although the article addresses water supply and sanitation access in Brazil (c1) and discusses institutional, concession, cost-recovery, and statutory frameworks including PLANASA and Law No. 11,445 of 2007 (c2), it is a non-empirical historical and public-policy overview essay. It presents no empirical study design, no primary qualitative or quantitative data, and no systematic empirical synthesis, relying solely on descriptive secondary statistics and policy commentary while noting that deeper methodological and case-study work is ongoing elsewhere. It is therefore excluded as E05 (No empirical evidence) under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Non-empirical narrative historical and public-policy overview
